site.title: The history of open source
site.tagline: From shared tapes to a contested label: how software that anyone may read, change and pass on came to run the world, told through the documents and the words of the people who were there.
one_screen: Software was shared before it was sold: IBM shipped its early programs as source code and its users, organised from 1955 as SHARE, swapped their changes [f:share-founded-1955] [f:share-library-source-form]. Unix was born at Bell Labs in 1969 [f:unix-born-1969] and Berkeley began sending out its own distribution in 1977 [f:bsd-first-distribution-1977]. The opposite view arrived in 1976, when Bill Gates told hobbyists that most of them were stealing their software [f:gates-open-letter-1976].

In September 1983 Richard Stallman announced GNU, a complete Unix-compatible system to be given away [f:gnu-announced-1983], and gave an ethical reason for it [f:gnu-golden-rule-1983]. The Free Software Foundation followed in 1985 [f:fsf-founded-1985], and the General Public License in 1989 used copyright to keep programs free [f:gpl-v1-1989] [f:copyleft-defined]. Linus Torvalds announced a hobby kernel in 1991 [f:linus-minix-post-1991] and put it under the GNU copyleft [f:linux-gpl-1992]; Debian wrote down what "free" meant in 1997 [f:debian-social-contract-1997].

The words "open source" date from February 1998 [f:open-source-label-osi-account]. Netscape had just announced it would publish its browser's source [f:netscape-announcement-1998]; Christine Peterson proposed the term [f:peterson-coins-open-source-1998], Eric Raymond campaigned for it [f:raymond-goodbye-free-software-1998], and he and Bruce Perens founded the Open Source Initiative with a definition adapted from Debian's guidelines [f:osi-founded-1998] [f:osd-derived-from-dfsg-1998]. Stallman does not accept the new name, because in his view it leaves out freedom [f:stallman-open-source-misses-point], and within a year Perens himself wrote that it was time to talk about free software again [f:perens-free-software-again-1999].

Microsoft treated the movement as a threat: a leaked 1998 memorandum called open source a direct, short-term revenue and platform threat [f:halloween-memo-threat-1998]; in 2001 Jim Allchin called it an intellectual-property destroyer [f:allchin-ip-destroyer-2001] and Steve Ballmer said Linux was a cancer in an intellectual property sense [f:ballmer-cancer-2001]; in 2007 the company claimed 235 of its patents were infringed [f:microsoft-235-patents-2007]. Meanwhile others bought in: IBM pledged $1 billion to Linux [f:ibm-billion-linux-2000], Sun freed StarOffice and Java [f:sun-staroffice-2000] [f:sun-java-gpl-2006], Google released Android [f:android-open-source-2008], and Git and GitHub changed how the work is done [f:git-created-2005] [f:github-launch-2008].

Then Microsoft turned: it contributed code to the Linux kernel under the GPL in 2009 [f:microsoft-linux-kernel-2009]; under Satya Nadella it showed a slide reading "Microsoft loves Linux" in 2014 [f:microsoft-loves-linux-2014], opened .NET [f:dotnet-open-source-2014], joined the Linux Foundation [f:microsoft-joins-linux-foundation-2016], bought GitHub for $7.5 billion [f:microsoft-github-announced-2018] and pledged 60,000 patents to protect Linux [f:microsoft-joins-oin-2018]. In 2020 its president said it had been on the wrong side of history [f:brad-smith-wrong-side-2020].

Since 2018 the argument has been over what the label still means: companies whose products were sold as cloud services by others have left open source licences [f:mongodb-sspl-2018] [f:elastic-licence-change-2021] [f:hashicorp-busl-2023] [f:redis-licence-change-2024], the OSI has said their new licences are not open source [f:osi-sspl-not-open-source-2021], open alternatives have been set up under the Linux Foundation [f:opentofu-2023] [f:valkey-2024] and two of the companies have come back [f:elastic-agpl-2024] [f:redis-agpl-2025]. Heartbleed, Log4Shell and the xz backdoor showed how much rests on a few maintainers [f:heartbleed-2014] [f:log4shell-2021] [f:xz-backdoor-2024], the European Union has legislated [f:cra-in-force-2024], and the OSI's definition of open source AI is disputed [f:osaid-1-0-2024] [f:sfc-osaid-criticism-2024].
state_now: The licence question is open again: MongoDB (2018), Elastic (2021), HashiCorp (2023) and Redis (2024) each moved a widely used product from an open source licence to one that restricts offering it as a service [f:mongodb-sspl-2018] [f:mongodb-sspl-cloud-reason-2018] [f:elastic-licence-change-2021] [f:hashicorp-busl-2023] [f:redis-licence-change-2024]. The Open Source Initiative holds that such licences are not open source, because the Open Source Definition forbids restricting fields of use [f:osi-sspl-not-open-source-2021] [f:osd-no-field-discrimination], and MongoDB's own FAQ says the SSPL is not OSI-approved [f:sspl-not-osi-approved].

Two of the changes were answered by a new project under the Linux Foundation: OpenTofu as an alternative to Terraform [f:opentofu-2023] and Valkey continuing Redis 7.2.4 [f:valkey-2024]. Two companies have since added an OSI-approved licence back: Elastic in August 2024 [f:elastic-agpl-2024] [f:elastic-open-source-again-2024] and Redis in May 2025, writing that the SSPL "is not truly open source" [f:redis-agpl-2025] [f:redis-sspl-not-truly-open-source-2025].

Security is now handled through shared bodies: after Heartbleed the Linux Foundation set up the Core Infrastructure Initiative [f:heartbleed-2014] [f:core-infrastructure-initiative-2014], which was folded into the Open Source Security Foundation in 2020 [f:openssf-founded-2020]. Log4Shell in 2021 was rated 10.0, critical [f:log4shell-2021], and in 2024 a backdoor was found in the upstream xz library [f:xz-backdoor-2024].

Regulation has arrived: the European Union's Cyber Resilience Act entered into force on 10 December 2024 [f:cra-in-force-2024]; it covers open source only where it is supplied commercially [f:cra-non-commercial-out-of-scope] and creates the category of open source software steward [f:cra-open-source-stewards], which the OSI welcomed [f:osi-on-cra-2024].

The newest dispute is over artificial intelligence: the OSI published its Open Source AI Definition 1.0 on 28 October 2024 [f:osaid-1-0-2024]; it asks for detailed information about training data rather than the data itself [f:osaid-data-information]. The Free Software Foundation says its own criteria will require the raw training data [f:fsf-ml-training-data-2024], and the Software Freedom Conservancy says the definition should not have been published yet [f:sfc-osaid-criticism-2024].

By GitHub's own count, more than 180 million developers now use its platform [f:octoverse-2025], and in 2024 they made more than 5.2 billion contributions, a figure that includes private projects [f:octoverse-2024]. Microsoft, which owns GitHub [f:microsoft-github-completed-2018], released the Windows Subsystem for Linux as open source in May 2025 [f:wsl-open-source-2025].

eras.title: Shared by default
eras.summary: Early software travelled as source code among the people who used the machines: IBM's users formed SHARE in 1955 [f:share-founded-1955] and exchanged their modifications [f:share-library-source-form]. Unix was born at Bell Labs in 1969 [f:unix-born-1969] and Berkeley's first distribution went out in 1977 [f:bsd-first-distribution-1977]. As software became a product, Bill Gates's 1976 letter put the case against sharing [f:gates-open-letter-1976].

eras.title: Free software
eras.summary: Richard Stallman announced GNU in 1983 [f:gnu-announced-1983], and the Free Software Foundation and the GPL gave the idea an organisation and a licence [f:fsf-founded-1985] [f:gpl-v1-1989]. Berkeley freed its code under permissive terms [f:bsd-networking-release-1989], Linux joined GNU under the copyleft [f:linux-gpl-1992], and Debian and Apache showed that volunteers could run large projects [f:debian-founded-1993] [f:apache-group-1995]. In 1997 Debian defined free software in its Social Contract [f:debian-social-contract-1997] and Eric Raymond described the method in "The Cathedral and the Bazaar" [f:cathedral-bazaar-1997].

eras.title: The label
eras.summary: Netscape's decision to publish its browser source [f:netscape-announcement-1998] prompted a new name, "open source", proposed by Christine Peterson [f:peterson-coins-open-source-1998] and promoted by Eric Raymond, Bruce Perens and Tim O'Reilly [f:osi-founded-1998] [f:open-source-summit-1998]. Stallman's movement kept the name free software [f:stallman-1998-splinter]. Microsoft's internal view leaked in the Halloween Documents [f:halloween-memo-threat-1998], while Red Hat went public and IBM and Sun committed to open source [f:red-hat-ipo-1999] [f:ibm-billion-linux-2000] [f:sun-staroffice-2000].

eras.title: Hostility and adoption
eras.summary: Microsoft's leaders attacked open source and the GPL in public in 2001 [f:allchin-ip-destroyer-2001] [f:mundie-gpl-viral-2001] [f:ballmer-cancer-2001], advertised against Linux [f:get-the-facts-2004] and claimed patent infringement [f:microsoft-235-patents-2007]; SCO sued IBM over Linux [f:sco-v-ibm-2003]. In the same years Firefox, Git, Android and GitHub appeared [f:firefox-1-0-2004] [f:git-created-2005] [f:android-announced-2007] [f:github-launch-2008], Sun put Java under the GPL [f:sun-java-gpl-2006] and the GPL reached version 3 [f:gplv3-released-2007].

eras.title: Mainstream
eras.summary: In these years even the largest opponent joined in: Microsoft contributed to the Linux kernel [f:microsoft-linux-kernel-2009] and, under Satya Nadella, declared that it loved Linux [f:nadella-ceo-2014] [f:microsoft-loves-linux-2014], opened .NET and Visual Studio Code [f:dotnet-open-source-2014] [f:vscode-open-source-2015] and joined the Linux Foundation [f:microsoft-joins-linux-foundation-2016]. Google open sourced Kubernetes, which then moved to a foundation [f:kubernetes-google-2014] [f:kubernetes-joins-cncf-2016]. Heartbleed showed the cost of depending on underfunded projects [f:heartbleed-2014].

eras.title: Strain and stewardship
eras.summary: Two of the largest open source companies were bought, GitHub by Microsoft and Red Hat by IBM [f:microsoft-github-announced-2018] [f:ibm-red-hat-closed-2019]. Vendors squeezed by cloud providers left open source licences and some returned [f:mongodb-sspl-2018] [f:redis-licence-change-2024] [f:elastic-agpl-2024]. Supply-chain attacks and vulnerabilities [f:log4shell-2021] [f:xz-backdoor-2024] brought foundations and regulators in [f:openssf-founded-2020] [f:cra-in-force-2024], and the meaning of "open source" for AI is contested [f:osaid-1-0-2024] [f:sfc-osaid-criticism-2024].

threads.title: From shared software to free software to open source
threads.intro: How a habit became a movement and then a label, and why the people who started the movement did not all accept the label.

steps.text: Software begins as something users exchange in source form.
Stallman finds the same habit at the MIT AI Lab and later takes it as his model.
Software becomes a product, and sharing it is called theft.
Stallman answers by announcing a complete free system, GNU.
His reason is ethical, not technical.
The Manifesto states the rule that redistribution may never be restricted.
The Free Software Foundation gives the project an organisation.
The GPL turns the rule into a licence.
A student announces a kernel as a hobby.
He puts it under the GNU copyleft.
GNU and Linux together make a complete free system.
Free software is defined by four freedoms.
Debian writes down what counts as free.
Raymond explains the method to outsiders.
A new name is proposed for the same software.
The case for the new name is that "free" confuses and alarms business.
The Open Source Definition is Debian's guidelines with Debian removed.
Stallman calls this a splintering of the community.
A co-founder of the OSI says the freedoms have been played down.
The free software position, in Stallman's words.
The GPL is revised to defend those freedoms against patents and locked devices.
The same disagreement reappears over machine learning.

threads.title: The label, 1998
threads.intro: Ten weeks, from Netscape's announcement to the summit that settled on the words "open source", followed step by step from the participants' own accounts.

steps.text: The essay that Netscape's managers read.
22 January: Netscape says it will publish its browser source.
It promises a licence in the tradition of the GPL.
Netscape's chief technology officer credits Raymond, by Raymond's account.
Early February: Christine Peterson thinks of "open source software".
A strategy meeting adopts it; Peterson dates it to 5 February.
The OSI's history dates the same step to 3 February.
8 February: Raymond publishes the call to switch terms.
Late February: Raymond and Perens found the Open Source Initiative.
Perens edits Debian's guidelines into the Open Source Definition.
The definition insists that open source is more than visible source code.
The Netscape code is released and the Mozilla project begins.
7 April: the leading developers agree on the term at O'Reilly's summit.
The meeting itself changes name, from Freeware Summit to Open Source Summit.
A year on, Perens leaves the OSI.

threads.title: The hostility
threads.intro: The case made against shared and open software by those who sold software, from 1976 to the lawsuits and campaigns of the 2000s, and how it ended.

steps.text: The first statement of the argument: sharing software is stealing.
The Unix owner's lawsuit against BSD ends with almost all the code cleared.
Microsoft's internal analysis names open source as a threat.
The same memo says the usual tactics will not work against it.
The memo leaks and, by Raymond's account, is acknowledged.
February 2001: the head of Windows calls open source an intellectual-property destroyer.
He wants policymakers warned.
May 2001: a set-piece speech attacks the GPL as viral.
June 2001: the chief executive calls Linux a cancer.
His explanation is about the licence.
SCO sues IBM, claiming rights over code in Linux.
Microsoft advertises against Linux.
Microsoft says open source infringes 235 of its patents.
Ballmer says open source users must play by the same rules.
Ballmer, retired, says the threat is behind Microsoft.
Microsoft acknowledges the friction over patents.
It puts its patents behind Linux instead.
The lawyer who made the 2007 patent claim says the company was wrong.
The SCO case is finally dismissed.

threads.title: Corporate adoption
threads.intro: How companies went from tolerating open source to building their businesses on it, and then to buying its institutions.

steps.text: Webmasters pool their patches and create the dominant web server.
A listed company opens its main product.
A Linux distributor becomes a public company.
Apache incorporates as a foundation.
Sun opens its office suite.
IBM commits $1 billion to Linux.
The opened Netscape code returns as Firefox.
The kernel developers build their own version control tool.
Google starts paying students to contribute.
Sun commits to releasing Java under the GPL.
Google and its partners announce an open mobile platform.
GitHub makes hosting and contributing a web service.
The Android source is published.
Google open sources Kubernetes.
It is released to the public in June.
A foundation is created for cloud infrastructure.
Kubernetes is handed to it.
Microsoft joins the Linux Foundation.
Microsoft buys the place where open source is developed.
IBM agrees to buy Red Hat.
The $34 billion deal closes.

threads.title: Microsoft and Linux: from "a cancer" to "Microsoft loves Linux"
threads.intro: One company's change of position, step by step, each step from a document: the leaked memo, the speeches and interviews of 2001, the first kernel contribution, the 2014 slide, and what followed.

steps.text: 1998: an internal memo sees a revenue and platform threat.
February 2001: "an intellectual-property destroyer".
May 2001: the GPL is called viral.
Microsoft offers "Shared Source" as its alternative.
June 2001: "a cancer that attaches itself in an intellectual property sense".
The remark is remembered in a shorter form than it was reported.
2004: an advertising campaign against Linux.
2007: the 235 patents claim.
July 2009: 20,000 lines of driver code for the Linux kernel, under the GPL.
Microsoft calls it its first contribution to the kernel.
September 2009: Microsoft funds an open source foundation.
2012: a subsidiary for open source and open standards.
February 2014: Satya Nadella becomes chief executive.
20 October 2014: "Microsoft loves Linux".
The words were a slide with a heart on it.
The stated reason: about a fifth of Azure already ran Linux.
November 2014: .NET is opened and brought to Linux.
May 2015: Microsoft repeats the slide in its own words.
November 2015: Visual Studio Code is open source.
March 2016: SQL Server for Linux is announced.
The same week Ballmer says the Linux threat is in the rearview mirror.
March 2016: Linux tools run inside Windows.
November 2016: platinum member of the Linux Foundation.
June 2018: the GitHub acquisition is announced.
October 2018: 60,000 patents pledged to protect Linux.
October 2018: the acquisition completes.
2020: "on the wrong side of history".
2025: the Windows Subsystem for Linux itself is open source.

threads.title: Licences and relicensing
threads.intro: The licences are the mechanism. This thread follows the two families, copyleft and permissive, the definitions built on them, and the recent moves away from both.

steps.text: The rule behind copyleft is stated.
Copyleft: copyright used to keep a program free.
GPL version 1.
Berkeley's first freely redistributable release.
GPL version 2, the licence Linux adopts.
Linux moves to the GNU copyleft.
The permissive alternative: keep the notices and the credit.
Debian's guidelines test whether a licence is free.
Netscape writes a new licence in the GPL's tradition.
The Open Source Definition becomes the test for "open source".
Its sixth criterion: no restriction on fields of use.
The GPL is attacked as viral.
A large company chooses the GPL for Java.
GPL version 3 adds patent and device provisions.
MongoDB writes the SSPL to reach cloud providers.
The SSPL is not OSI-approved.
Elastic leaves the Apache licence.
The OSI says the SSPL is not open source.
The SSPL had been withdrawn from OSI review.
HashiCorp moves Terraform to the Business Source License.
OpenTofu is launched as an open source alternative, from a fork of Terraform.
Redis leaves the BSD licence.
Valkey continues the last BSD-licensed Redis.
Elastic adds the AGPL.
Redis adds the AGPL.
Redis concedes the SSPL is not truly open source.

threads.title: Security and sustainability
threads.intro: The promise that many eyes make bugs shallow, and what happened when critical projects turned out to have very few eyes on them.

steps.text: The promise: given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow.
Heartbleed: a serious flaw in a library the internet depends on.
Industry funds critical projects in response.
The effort is consolidated in the Open Source Security Foundation.
Log4Shell: a critical flaw in a ubiquitous logging library.
A deliberate backdoor is found in xz.
The European Union legislates on software security.
The law gives open source foundations a defined role.

threads.title: Where things stand
threads.intro: The open questions of 2018 to 2026, each from the statements of the parties.

steps.text: The vendors' complaint: cloud providers sell their software as a service.
The rule their new licences break.
The OSI's ruling.
The community response: an open source alternative under a foundation.
The same response to Redis.
The supply chain is attacked through an upstream project.
Elastic returns to an OSI-approved licence.
European law defines open source stewards.
Non-commercial open source stays outside the law.
The OSI defines open source AI.
It asks for information about training data.
The FSF wants the data itself.
The Software Freedom Conservancy says the definition erodes the term.
The scale, in GitHub's numbers for 2024.
Redis returns to an OSI-approved licence.
Microsoft opens the Windows Subsystem for Linux.
GitHub counts more than 180 million developers.

threads.title: Where open source meets Agile
threads.intro: The two histories share people, tools and one habit: put working software in front of others early and often. Each step here is a point where they touch.

steps.text: A future Agile Manifesto author starts the first wiki.
Two programmers write JUnit, the tool behind test-first development.
Raymond states the bazaar's rule: release early, release often.
Fowler lists open source among the new methods.
He notes that its debugging runs in parallel.
The first continuous integration article builds on an open source tool.
Beck, Cunningham and Fowler sign the Agile Manifesto.
The Manifesto asks to be copied freely.
The first continuous integration server is an open source project.
The Linux kernel's needs produce Git.
GitHub adds the pull request.
DevOps gets its conference.
DevOps is described as Agile applied to operations.
The Hudson community votes to become Jenkins.
Jenkins and GitHub Actions are named as usual continuous integration services.

disputed.title: "Free software" versus "open source"
disputed.summary: The two terms cover almost the same programs but not the same idea [f:stallman-open-source-misses-point]. Raymond argued in 1998 that "free software" was ambiguous and made business nervous [f:raymond-free-software-term-has-to-go]. Stallman holds that open source values practical advantage and leaves out freedom, and the GNU Project does not use the term [f:stallman-open-source-misses-point] [f:stallman-1998-splinter]. Perens, who wrote the Open Source Definition, said in 1999 that the two were the same thing but that open source had played down the freedoms [f:perens-free-software-again-1999] [f:perens-leaves-osi-1999]. The dispute is one of values, not of fact [f:stallman-open-source-misses-point].

disputed.title: Who coined "open source", and when
disputed.summary: The OSI credits Christine Peterson with suggesting the term [f:open-source-label-osi-account], and she has published her own account of coming up with it [f:peterson-coins-open-source-1998]. Raymond's call of 8 February 1998 says "we came up with" the label and does not name her [f:raymond-goodbye-free-software-1998]. The date of the meeting is not settled by the sources: the OSI says 3 February 1998 [f:open-source-label-osi-account], while Peterson's narrative says 5 February [f:open-source-meeting-peterson-account] and Raymond's text also points to 5 February [f:raymond-goodbye-free-software-1998]. Peterson says it was Todd Anderson who put the term to the meeting [f:open-source-meeting-peterson-account].

disputed.title: What Steve Ballmer said about Linux in 2001
disputed.summary: The usual quotation is "Linux is a cancer" [f:ballmer-cancer-short-form]. The sentence as reported is longer: "Linux is a cancer that attaches itself in an intellectual property sense to everything it touches" [f:ballmer-cancer-2001], and his explanation was about the terms of the licence [f:ballmer-cancer-licence-context-2001]. The short form is a headline [f:ballmer-cancer-short-form]. The words come from a Chicago Sun-Times interview of 1 June 2001, which could not be read for this site; they are quoted here from The Register's report of the next day [f:ballmer-cancer-2001]. In 2016 Ballmer was reported as saying the position had been right for its time [f:ballmer-rearview-2016], wording that is the reporter's paraphrase.

disputed.title: Who made the 235 patents claim
disputed.summary: The claim that free and open source software infringes 235 Microsoft patents is often put in Ballmer's mouth [f:microsoft-235-patents-2007]. Fortune's article attributes the figure to Brad Smith and Horacio Gutierrez [f:microsoft-235-patents-2007]; Ballmer is quoted in the same article on playing by the same rules [f:ballmer-same-rules-2007]. Microsoft later acknowledged friction over patents when it joined the Open Invention Network [f:microsoft-oin-friction-2018].

disputed.title: Whether Microsoft acknowledged the Halloween memorandum
disputed.summary: Raymond states that Microsoft admitted the memorandum was authentic [f:halloween-authenticity-1998]. That statement is his, and the memorandum itself is read in his annotated copy [f:halloween-memo-threat-1998].

disputed.title: Whether source-available licences are open source
disputed.summary: MongoDB presented the SSPL as an open source licence and submitted it to the OSI [f:mongodb-sspl-2018] [f:mongodb-sspl-cloud-reason-2018]. The OSI says it is not open source, because it restricts a field of use, and that it was withdrawn from review [f:osi-sspl-not-open-source-2021] [f:osi-sspl-withdrawn] [f:osd-no-field-discrimination]. The companies' own later statements concede the point about the label: MongoDB's FAQ says the SSPL is not OSI-approved [f:sspl-not-osi-approved], Elastic said an OSI-approved licence was what let it use the term again [f:elastic-open-source-again-2024], and Redis wrote that the SSPL is not truly open source [f:redis-sspl-not-truly-open-source-2025]. The opponents of HashiCorp's change call the Business Source License non-open source [f:hashicorp-busl-2023]; HashiCorp's own statement could not be read. What remains disputed is whether the OSI's definition should be the only test of the label [f:osi-sspl-not-open-source-2021].

disputed.title: The Open Source AI Definition
disputed.summary: The OSI's definition requires detailed information about training data, not the data [f:osaid-1-0-2024] [f:osaid-data-information]. The Free Software Foundation says a free machine learning application must provide the raw training data [f:fsf-ml-training-data-2024]. The Software Freedom Conservancy says the definition fails to require reproducibility and should have been held back [f:sfc-osaid-criticism-2024].

disputed.title: Stallman's role and the name "GNU/Linux"
disputed.summary: The GNU Project says that by 1990 it had written or found every major part of a free system except the kernel, and that Linux completed it, so the combined system should be called GNU/Linux [f:gnu-plus-linux-1992]. Torvalds's own first announcement set his kernel beside GNU, "won't be big and professional like gnu" [f:linus-minix-post-1991], and he adopted the GNU copyleft [f:linux-gpl-1992]. Only the GNU Project's side of the naming argument is sourced here [f:gnu-plus-linux-1992]: no statement by Torvalds on the name was fetched.

disputed.title: "Given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow"
disputed.summary: Raymond named this "Linus's Law", but the wording is his own [f:linuss-law-1997]. Heartbleed, Log4Shell and the xz backdoor are the usual evidence that widely used code does not always have enough eyes on it [f:heartbleed-2014] [f:log4shell-2021] [f:xz-backdoor-2024]; the xz backdoor was also found by one person who noticed odd behaviour and traced it [f:xz-backdoor-2024].

disputed.title: What the April 1998 summit was called
disputed.summary: The same meeting is the "Freeware Summit" in its advance announcement and the "Open Source Summit" a week later, by Peterson's account [f:freeware-summit-renamed-1998]; O'Reilly's press release speaks of open source pioneers [f:open-source-summit-1998]; the OSI's history calls it the "Free Software Summit" [f:open-source-label-osi-account].

bridge.text: Raymond's rule for the bazaar, written in 1997, sits beside the iterative delivery that Agile asked for four years later: release often and listen to the people who use the software.
The essay that named the bazaar style is where "release early, release often" comes from.
Ward Cunningham, an author of the Agile Manifesto, built the first wiki as a supplement to the Portland Pattern Repository.
The word "wiki" is Cunningham's, in his own words.
Cunningham's later wiki work is itself open source, under the MIT licence or the GPL.
JUnit was written by Kent Beck, an Agile Manifesto author, with Erich Gamma, pair programmed and test first by Fowler's account.
JUnit is distributed under an open source licence.
Seven months before the Agile Manifesto, Martin Fowler listed open source next to XP, Scrum and the other light methods as a way of working worth learning from.
Fowler took from open source the same observation Raymond called Linus's Law.
Continuous integration, an Extreme Programming practice, was built from the start on open source tools.
Three of the seventeen authors of the Manifesto appear in the history of open source for their own tools and writing.
The Manifesto's own notice lets anyone copy it, though only whole: the wish to be passed on is shared with open source, the freedom to modify is not.
The first continuous integration server came from Thoughtworks, Fowler's employer, and was open source.
CruiseControl was registered as a BSD-licensed project in March 2001, a month after the Manifesto.
Git was made for the Linux kernel; GitHub built the pull request on it, and Fowler's account of continuous integration now assumes both.
The pull request began as a GitHub feature for telling others to pull your changes; Fowler's 2024 article on continuous integration has a section on how pull requests fit with it.
DevOps took a name and a conference in 2009.
DevOps was described at the time as Agile and Lean approaches carried into operations.
A continuous integration server is governed by its open source community, which chose its own name by vote.
Fowler's current account of continuous integration names Jenkins and GitHub Actions as the usual services.
